findings.evidence: "stated here at first use, defined in full at Ch 8 §8.3.3"
findings.issue: Section reference 'Ch 8 §8.3.3' violates the book's own cross-reference convention stated on PDF p.19: "Do not repeat a chapter number after the chapter name — write Ch. 8 § 3 or § 8.3.3, not Ch. 8 § 8.3.3." The chapter number 8 appears both before and inside the section reference.
findings.fix_instruction: Change to '§ 8.3.3' (standalone) or 'Ch. 8 § 3.3' (chapter-first, section number only), per the stated convention.

findings.evidence: "not the per-host aggregate rate of ~19,800 tok/s — see Ch 8 §8.3.4"
findings.issue: Section reference 'Ch 8 §8.3.4' violates the same cross-reference convention (PDF p.19: 'not Ch. 8 § 8.3.3'). The chapter number 8 appears before and inside the reference. This is the second instance of the same defect pattern.

findings.evidence: Page 43, Table 2-2 row: "Decode: required bandwidth, hypothetical single-device aggregate (TPOT ~25 ms) | 5.6 TB/s | 140 GB / 0.025 s — the whole model read once per step on one device (batch-1-equivalent weight-streaming model, before amortization); an aggregate figure, not a per-GPU one [canonical scenario][DERIVED]". Page 44 row: "Decode: bandwidth verdict, hypothetical single-device aggregate | bandwidth-bound | 5.6 > 3.35 → one device holding the whole 140 GB model cannot meet the demand. This row compares aggregate bytes against a single device's bandwidth, and a 140-GB FP16 model does not fit on one 80-GB H100: the row illustrates the roofline point, not a deployable layout". Page 49: "140 GB / 0.025 s = 5,600 GB/s = 5.6 TB/s ... Since 5.6 > 3.35, under this batch-1-equivalent weight-streaming model one H100 cannot supply the required aggregate weight-read rate — the decode phase is HBM-bandwidth-bound".
findings.issue: The 5.6 TB/s figure is carried as [canonical scenario][DERIVED] on p. 43 and repeatedly on p. 49, but it describes a hypothetical single-device layout that the book itself says is not deployable ('a 140-GB FP16 model does not fit on one 80-GB H100') and that no canonical scenario field specifies. Under the book's own Axis-1 definitions it is a non-canonical hypothetical worked example and should be [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. The same page-43 row also carries the canonical label onto a figure whose denominator ('one device') contradicts the canonical deployment unit (8×H100, p. 42: 'a 70B-class dense model in FP16, 1 host with 8×H100 GPUs').
findings.fix_instruction: Retag the 5.6 TB/s single-device aggregate row and its derived verdict as [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (with the label also stating 'hypothetical single-device, not deployable'), and keep [canonical scenario][DERIVED] only for the sharded per-GPU row (700 GB/s per GPU) that matches the canonical 8×H100 host.

findings.evidence: Page 44: "Decode: required bandwidth per GPU (sharded, TP = 8) | 700 GB/s per GPU | 17.5 GB / 0.025 s, where 70B / 8 = 8.75B params = 17.5 GB shard per GPU per step. Same per-GPU denominator as the 3.35 TB/s peak, so the two rows are directly comparable". Page 49: "the shard streams in ~5.2 ms at peak, 21% of the 25 ms TPOT step".
findings.issue: The verdict row on p. 44 is labeled 'bandwidth-feasible' on the strength of 700 GB/s < 3.35 TB/s, and p. 49 repeats '~5.2 ms at peak, 21% of the 25 ms TPOT step' — but at 21% of peak HBM utilization this is a batch-1-equivalent read with no batching amortization and no TP-collective, kernel-launch, sampling or scheduling overhead. The book elsewhere (p. 50) warns 'the canonical 25 ms TPOT is a budget covering TP collectives, kernel inefficiency, sampling and scheduling, not a bandwidth-saturated point' (p. 137, Ch. 6). Table 2-2's 'bandwidth-feasible' verdict is therefore presented as a sufficiency conclusion where the underlying arithmetic only establishes 'bandwidth is not the binding constraint at this point' — the two are different claims, and p. 50 itself says the real saturation threshold 'must be measured rather than read off either subset'.
findings.fix_instruction: Rename the p. 44 verdict row from 'bandwidth-feasible' to 'bandwidth not binding at this point (batch-1-equivalent, ~21% of peak)' and add the p. 50 caveat in the same cell, so the table does not assert a sufficiency verdict the chapter's own text disclaims.

findings.evidence: Page 45: "Prefill: FLOPs, linear term only (2 × params × tokens) | 1.29 PFLOP | 2 ×70e9 ×9.2e3 ≈ 1.29 ×10¹⁵; excludes the quadratic attention term, which adds ~0.22 PFLOP (+17%) at 9.2K → ~1.51 PFLOP total, Ch 8 case (ii) [canonical scenario][DERIVED]". Page 45 also: "Prefill: regime verdict | compute-bound regime | weight-only arithmetic intensity ~9.2K FLOP/byte ... including it, ~7,850 FLOP/byte (Ch 8)".
findings.issue: The stated attention term is ~0.22 PFLOP and the total ~1.51 PFLOP, implying 1.29 + 0.22 = 1.51 — but the book's own case-(iii) figure (p. 45 scope note) is ~1.40 PFLOP for the causal-triangle term, and Ch. 8's case-(ii) formula (p. 174) is '4·n_layers·L²·d'. Recomputing: 4 × 80 × 9,200² × 8,192 = 4 × 80 × 84,640,000 × 8,192 ≈ 2.219×10¹⁵ = ~2.22 PFLOP, not ~0.22 PFLOP — a factor of ten. Even the causal-triangle variant (2 × 80 × 9,200² × 8,192) ≈ 1.11 PFLOP, giving ~2.40 PFLOP total, not ~1.40. The figure is also given as '+17%' (0.22/1.29 = 17.1%), which is internally consistent with 0.22 but not with the formula the book states for it. The consequence propagates: p. 46 says 'with the attention term included (~1.51 PFLOP) the demand is ~1.40 PFLOPS' — but 1.51/1.08 = 1.40 PFLOPS, so this row uses 1.51 while claiming to be the case-(ii) total, whereas p. 45's scope note says case (ii) total is ~1.51 and case (iii) is ~1.40 — the two are swapped.
findings.fix_instruction: Recompute the quadratic attention term from the book's own stated formula (4·n_layers·L²·d at 80 layers, L=9,200, d=8,192) and restate the case-(ii) and case-(iii) totals, the percentage, and the derived PFLOPS demand (~1.19 → the corrected figure) consistently in Table 2-2, its scope note, p. 46 and p. 49. If the intended formula differs from the one printed on p. 174, fix the formula in Ch. 8 and state which single convention the book uses for the prefill FLOP figure.

findings.evidence: Page 46: "Prefill: single-H100 capacity | insufficient for real-time prefill | 1.29 PFLOP / ~1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS demand > 0.989 PFLOPS H100 peak". Page 49: "rate = 1.29 PFLOP / 1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS".
findings.issue: Both instances use 1.29 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s. 1.29/1.08 = 1.194 — correct. However the row's own text says the prefill budget is a 'two-term-only upper cap' whose feasible form is 'budget_prefill ≤ 1.08 s − B_other' (p. 19, p. 94). Dividing by 1.08 s therefore computes the demand rate against a budget that is known to be too large, which understates the required rate (a smaller allowed time implies a larger demand). The book flags this in the Table 4-2 row but the arithmetic in Ch. 2 proceeds as though 1.08 s were the allocation, and the p. 45 row 'Prefill: regime verdict' inherits the same figure.
findings.fix_instruction: State the ~1.19 PFLOPS as a lower bound on the required rate (computed against the 1.08 s upper cap, so the true demand rate is ≥1.19 PFLOPS), and add the same one-line caveat that p. 19 and p. 94 give, directly in Table 2-2's derivation cell.

findings.evidence: Page 49: "On the canonical 8×H100 host (TP = 8): prefill 1.29 PFLOP / (8 × 0.989 PFLOPS) = 0.16 s at peak, ~0.47 s at 35% MFU, inside the 1.08 s budget ... decode shard 70B/8 = 8.75B params = 17.5 GB/GPU per step → 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.2 ms at peak, inside the 25 ms TPOT budget ... KV 24.1 GB per request (24.9 GB on the 9.5K-token slot-counting basis) against the 640 GB pool. Two KV bases, named: at the pre-generation 9.2K-input point the request's KV is 24.1 GB, so the host footprint is ~228 GB (140 GB weights + ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve + 24.1 GB KV); at the end-of-generation 9.5K resident basis the same host holds ~229 GB (140 + 64 + 24.9 GB — the figure Ch 7 Fig 7.8 uses)."
findings.issue: The two KV bases are named but the two host-footprint totals are presented as distinct figures (~228 GB vs ~229 GB) when the arithmetic gives 140 + 64 + 24.1 = 228.1 and 140 + 64 + 24.9 = 228.9. Fig 7.8 (p. 172) prints '228.9 GB at 9.5K (shown as 229)'. So the ~228 figure is 228.1 and the ~229 figure is 228.9 — but both are shown as three-significant-digit integers, making the '24.9 GB on the 9.5K-token slot-counting basis' and the '24.1 GB' basis differ by only 1 GB while being called out as two named bases. More importantly, the ~64 GB runtime reserve is introduced here for the first time in Ch. 2 without provenance in the same sentence; it is tagged only later (p. 124: '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] The ~64 GB is a planning reserve, not a measured constant'). The p. 49 paragraph carries no tag at all for the ~228/~229 GB figures.
findings.fix_instruction: Add the [canonical scenario][DERIVED] tag to the ~228.1 / ~228.9 GB footprint sentence and an inline pointer to the reserve's assumption tag (Ch. 7 §7.1), or move the reserve's first introduction into Ch. 2 with its tag so the number never appears untagged before its provenance is stated.

findings.evidence: Page 50: "At the canonical operating point the 5.2 ms weight read moves 21% of peak over the 25 ms step ... it saturates HBM above ~5 concurrent sequences per GPU (~40 per host) only in the no-amortization case where each sequence streams its own full 17.5 GB shard, with no weight-read amortization. Under amortized batching that read is shared across the batch, so the weight-matmul portion stays bandwidth-bound up to ~295 concurrent sequences per GPU (~2,360 per host) — the point where its arithmetic intensity (B tokens ≈ B FLOP/byte) reaches the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge and it becomes compute-bound."
findings.issue: The '~295 concurrent sequences per GPU' figure is obtained by setting the batch's arithmetic intensity B FLOP/byte equal to the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge. But the roofline ridge is H100's ratio of peak FLOPs to peak bandwidth (0.989 PFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOP/byte) for BF16 dense. A batch of B tokens at FP16/FP8 has per-token FLOPs of 140 GFLOP and per-token weight bytes of 140 GB shared across the batch, so intensity = 140·B GFLOP / 140 GB = B FLOP/byte — the derivation is right. The defect is the omission of the KV traffic term: the same paragraph immediately states the attention portion 'reads KV cache at an intensity of only ~1 FLOP/byte ... and stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size', so the combined step intensity at B = 295 is nowhere near the ridge. The paragraph therefore presents '295 concurrent sequences per GPU' as the compute-bound threshold without the KV term it introduces two sentences later, and Ch. 6 (p. 137) gives the corrected combined figure: 'intensity saturates at ~6.8 FLOP/byte ... ~5.8 at batch 32' — i.e. never reaching the ridge at any realistic batch.
findings.fix_instruction: Either add the KV term to the intensity used for the threshold (so the batch never reaches the ridge at realistic B), or explicitly mark the ~295-per-GPU figure as the weight-matmul-portion-only bound that the next sentence disqualifies — matching Ch. 6's combined-intensity figure.

findings.evidence: Page 43 Table 2-2 row: "Model weight bytes (FP16) | 140 GB | 2 bytes × 70B params [canonical scenario][DERIVED]". Page 55 (Ch. 3 Table 3-1): "FP16 residency (total) | 140 GB | 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB [canonical scenario][DERIVED]". Page 93 (Ch. 4 Table 4-2): "Model parameters | 70B | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] reference model".
findings.issue: The parameter count 70B is an assumed input ([canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]) but the byte figure 140 GB is repeatedly tagged [canonical scenario][DERIVED] — correct per the book's own convention (p. 17: 'an input or parameter assumption ... is [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]; a value arithmetically derived from those assumed inputs ... is [canonical scenario][DERIVED]'). However Ch. 3's Table 3-1 (p. 59) labels the 70B itself as '70B | canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2) | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] reference model' while the same table's 'Active parameters per token | 70B | All parameters active for every token (dense) | [canonical scenario][DERIVED]' — the latter derives a fact about dense-ness from the label 'dense 70B' in the same table. These are internally consistent, but the Table 3-1 geometry rows ('layers 80', 'hidden_dim 8192') are not present in that table at all, while Ch. 7 (p. 146) introduces them as 'canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference model' and Table 4-2 (p. 92) lists them with [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]. The teaching geometry is therefore introduced as a Ch. 7 object while Ch. 3's parameter table already uses it — a forward reference without a pointer.
findings.fix_instruction: In Ch. 3 Table 3-1, either add the layer/hidden/head rows (with their [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] tags, cross-referenced to Table 4-2) or add an explicit 'geometry per Ch. 4 Table 4-2 / Ch. 7 §7.3' pointer in the table header so the reader is not asked to accept an unstated geometry in a parameter table.

findings.evidence: Page 50: "Under amortized batching that read is shared across the batch, so the weight-matmul portion stays bandwidth-bound up to ~295 concurrent sequences per GPU (~2,360 per host) — the point where its arithmetic intensity (B tokens ≈ B FLOP/byte) reaches the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge and it becomes compute-bound. Neither number describes the full decode step: the attention portion reads KV cache at an intensity of only ~1 FLOP/byte for the full-MHA canonical model (~8 FLOP/byte for an 8:1 GQA geometry) and stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size, so the real saturation threshold, which includes KV traffic (~3.01 GB/seq at the 9.2K input context per GPU), must be measured rather than read off either subset."
findings.issue: Recompute the attention intensity. For one decode step over a cache of L tokens, full dense attention: FLOPs = 2 (QK^T) + 2 (AV) × L × d_model per layer = 4·L·d_model; bytes = 2 (K and V) × L × d_model. Ratio = 2 FLOP/byte exactly, independent of L and of the model's layer count. For GQA-8 (d_kv = 8×128 = 1,024 vs d_model 8,192), FLOPs = 4·L·d_model (query is full width) but bytes = 2·L·d_kv, so ratio = 2 × 8,192/1,024 = 16 FLOP/byte. The book states ~1 FLOP/byte for full-MHA and ~8 FLOP/byte for GQA-8 — both exactly half the correct values (2 and 16), consistent with counting only one of the two matmuls. And the conclusion 'stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size' does not follow from either figure: 2 FLOP/byte (full-MHA) is below the 295 ridge but 16 FLOP/byte (GQA-8) is also below it — however the book's own arithmetic (1 or 8) is what it reasons from, and Ch. 6 §6.3.3 compounds the error into the '~6.8 FLOP/byte' saturation claim.
findings.fix_instruction: Correct the attention intensities to 2 FLOP/byte (full-MHA) and 16 FLOP/byte (GQA-8), derived as 4·L·d_model FLOPs over 2·L·d_kv bytes, and recompute the batch-size saturation and the 'bandwidth-bound at every batch size' conclusion in Ch. 2 §2.3 and Ch. 6 §6.3.3 from the corrected figures.

findings.evidence: Page 42: "To make the distinction concrete, let us walk through the canonical enterprise Q&A scenario from canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): a 70B-class dense model in FP16, 1 host with 8×H100 GPUs, prompt of 1,200 tokens + 8K retrieved context (~9.2K input), 300-token output, TTFT budget 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill), TPOT budget ~25 ms/token."
findings.issue: The phrase 'from canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2)' uses 'canonical scenario' as a preposition-like phrase ('from the canonical scenario'), but 'canonical scenario' is one of the book's Axis-1 provenance tags in square brackets elsewhere. Used without brackets here it reads as a garbled sentence fragment ('walk through the canonical enterprise Q&A scenario from canonical scenario'), and the reader may briefly parse 'canonical scenario' as a second scenario rather than as the tag. The same unmarked usage appears on p. 111 ('canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2)') in a running-head context and in Ch. 3 (p. 59: 'We now carry concrete arithmetic using the canonical enterprise Q&A scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2)').
findings.fix_instruction: Either bracket the tag ([canonical scenario]) or rephrase to 'walk through the canonical enterprise Q&A scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)', so the Axis-1 vocabulary is never used unbracketed as a sentence fragment.

findings.evidence: Page 38, Table 2-1 rows: 'compute capacity | FLOP/s | how much arithmetic per unit time | prefill (Ch. 2, 8)'; 'memory bandwidth | bytes/s | how fast data can move | decode (Ch. 2, 8)'; 'memory capacity | bytes resident | how much state fits (weights + KV) | KV cache / concurrency (Ch. 7)'; 'interconnect bandwidth/latency | bytes/s, delay | cross-GPU / cross-host movement | communication (Ch. 9) and parallelism (Ch. 10)'; 'scheduling capacity | useful work resident | keeping hardware busy despite request raggedness | serving (Ch. 11)'; 'latency budget | TTFT, TPOT/ITL, end-to-end | the SLO the system must meet | workload (Ch. 4)'; 'throughput / goodput | useful tokens/s under SLO | completed work, not just tokens/s | metrics (Ch. 6)'.
findings.issue: The table's 'first surfaces in' column lists 'prefill (Ch. 2, 8)' and 'decode (Ch. 2, 8)' — the citation form is bare chapter numbers without the book's stated cross-reference format. The Preface (p. 20) defines the section-reference form '§ N.M' and the chapter-naming form 'Ch. 7 § 3'; bare parenthetical chapter lists '(Ch. 2, 8)' and '(Ch. 9)' are used pervasively throughout the book (e.g. p. 38 '(Ch. 9) and parallelism (Ch. 10)'; p. 39 'serving (Ch. 11)'; p. 137 '(Ch. 11 lists [S1]–[S6] inline)'; p. 111 '(Ch 8/16–17)'). More substantively, the 'scheduling capacity' row's unit 'useful work resident' is not a unit in the same class as the others (FLOP/s, bytes/s, bytes resident, bytes/s delay, TTFT, tokens/s) — it is a descriptor of a quantity ('useful work resident' is missing its unit entirely), and 'latency budget' likewise has no unit. Two of the seven rows therefore cannot be checked against the resource model's claim that each resource 'names one constraint'.
findings.fix_instruction: Give every row in Table 2-1 a measurable unit — e.g. 'scheduling capacity | resident sequences (slot count)' and 'latency budget | s (TTFT, TPOT/ITL, end-to-end)' — and normalize the 'first surfaces in' column to the book's declared cross-reference form ('§ 2, § 8').

findings.evidence: Page 39: "The causal chain (how the chapters hold together). The book is one argument, not a set of topics. The thread is: tokens determine sequence length → sequence length determines KV growth and attention work → KV growth determines memory pressure → attention and model execution determine compute and bandwidth demand → those resource demands determine latency behavior → latency and concurrency determine scheduler requirements → scheduler behavior determines serving efficiency → serving efficiency and SLOs determine host count → host count and model topology determine interconnect and fleet architecture → fleet architecture determines cost, resilience, placement, and operational complexity."
findings.issue: The chain is stated as the book's spine, and the Contents (p. 6–7) organizes Part I–VI as Token / Workload / System / Architecture / Fleet / Architect. But the chain places 'host count' (Ch. 17) before 'fleet architecture' (Ch. 16/17) and 'cost' last, while the Preface's own decision loop (p. 14, Fig 1) sequences 'Validate & Defend: TCO' before 'Commit: red team', and the Preface's operational checklist (p. 13) puts 'How many hosts?' (Q4) before 'Who serves it?' (Q5) — a different order from the chain, which puts scheduler requirements before host count. The book presents both as the spine, and they are not the same sequence, without stating which is normative.
findings.fix_instruction: State explicitly in Ch. 2 §2.1 that the causal chain describes physical dependency while the Preface's six-question checklist describes the architect's working order, and note where the two diverge (host count vs scheduler requirements) so a reader does not treat two different 'spines' as one.

findings.evidence: Page 47, Fig 2.2: the roofline plot shows 'roofline ridge ~295', 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte', with 'decode' plotted at ~1 FLOP/byte and 'prefill' at the high-intensity end. Caption: 'Low-batch decode (streaming weights per token) lands at ~1 FLOP/byte ... long-prompt prefill lands at high intensity ... markers = regime, not measured MFU (real kernels run below the roof)'.
findings.issue: Recompute the ridge: 989 TFLOPS ÷ 3.35 TB/s = 989,000/3,350 = 295.2 FLOP/byte ✓. The decode marker at ~1 FLOP/byte: for the weight-read-only approximation, 140 GFLOP ÷ 140 GB = 1.0 ✓. The prefill marker at ~9,200 FLOP/byte ✓. The figure's vertical axis is labelled 'attainable performance (FLOP/s)' with ticks 1e+11 to 1e+15 — but the H100's peak is 989 TFLOPS = 9.89e14, which falls between the 1e+14 and 1e+15 ticks, and the ridge annotation line is drawn accordingly. The defect: the figure plots the *weight-only* intensities (1 and 9,200 FLOP/byte) while Ch. 2's own text (p. 47, the paragraph below the figure) states 'weight-only arithmetic intensity places the canonical prefill point ~9.2K FLOP/byte (~7,850 FLOP/byte once the ~24 GB KV write is counted, Ch 8)'. The figure therefore shows the prefill marker at a position the text corrects two lines later, without any note on the figure itself that the marker is weight-only.
findings.fix_instruction: Add a note to Fig 2.2's caption (or to the prefill marker label) that the plotted intensities are weight-only, with the KV-write-adjusted value (~7,850 FLOP/byte) given in the caption, so the figure's marker position is not read as the full-traffic intensity.

findings.evidence: Page 49: "decode shard 70B/8 = 8.75B params = 17.5 GB/GPU per step → 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.2 ms at peak". Recompute: 17.5 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s = 17.5/3350 s = 5.22 ms ✓. Page 49 also: "at 60–80% of peak the same shard takes ~8.7–6.5 ms" — 17.5/0.6/3350 = 8.7 ms ✓; 17.5/0.8/3350 = 6.5 ms ✓. Page 44 Table 2-2: "700 GB/s per GPU | 17.5 GB / 0.025 s" ✓.
findings.issue: The decode arithmetic is consistent and correctly caveated. The defect is that the canonical TPOT budget of 25 ms is compared against a weight-read time of 5.2 ms (21%) with the verdict 'inside the 25 ms TPOT budget' — while the same host's decode must also perform the per-token attention over the 9.2K-token KV cache and the TP all-reduce for 8 ranks, and the book's own p. 50 text says the real saturation threshold 'must be measured'. The 'bandwidth-feasible' verdict on p. 44 therefore compares a partial step against the full budget. The book flags this in Ch. 6's table footnote ('the canonical 25 ms TPOT is a budget covering TP collectives, kernel inefficiency, sampling and scheduling, not a bandwidth-saturated point') but the verdict cell itself does not.
findings.fix_instruction: Add to Table 2-2's per-GPU verdict cell the explicit scope note that only the weight-read component is compared against the 25 ms budget, and that attention, collectives and scheduling remain unaccounted — cross-referencing Ch. 6's footnote so the verdict is not read as a full-step feasibility result.

findings.evidence: Page 37–38 vocabulary table: 'KV offloading | moving some KV state out of GPU HBM (to host DRAM/SSD), trading capacity against transfer latency | not shrinking the state itself'. Page 164 (Ch. 7 §7.7): "(a) decode-time KV offload to CPU DRAM trades TPOT/ITL and KV capacity, not TTFT (TTFT is already complete when decode starts)". Page 139 (Ch. 6 §6.6): "vLLM KV-offloading (its own 2026-01-08 blog [S7][1P][FACT]) cuts TTFT by 2–22× in a particular warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark".
findings.issue: The book's vocabulary table (p. 37) binds KV offloading to 'trading capacity against transfer latency' and Ch. 7 (p. 164) is precise that decode-time offload trades TPOT/ITL and capacity, not TTFT. But Ch. 6 (p. 139) cites a vLLM blog claiming offloading 'cuts TTFT by 2–22×' — which, if true, is a different mechanism (prefix/KV reuse loaded from CPU for cache-hit requests) than the decode-time offload the vocabulary table describes. Ch. 6's own sentence does distinguish them ('in a particular warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark'), and Ch. 7 (p. 164) also separates them ('(b) prefix/KV reuse loaded from CPU can reduce TTFT for cache-hit requests'). But Ch. 6's bullet heading is 'KV cache pressure ⇒ quantize or offload KV', which presents the TTFT claim under the decode-offload lever without the distinction the chapter's own vocabulary demands.
findings.fix_instruction: Split Ch. 6 §6.6's KV-offload bullet into two labelled mechanisms — 'decode-time KV offload (capacity ↔ TPOT/ITL)' and 'prefix/KV reuse from CPU (TTFT on cache hits)' — so the 2–22× TTFT figure is not attached to the mechanism the vocabulary table defines as capacity-vs-latency.

findings.evidence: Page 40, Fig 2.1 caption: 'PREFILL (top) is the one-shot parallel pass over the whole prompt; it populates the persistent KV cache and is the dominant contributor to TTFT (time to first token — though TTFT also includes queueing, preprocessing, and transport, so model prefill latency is a component of, not identical to, user-observed TTFT). DECODE (bottom) is the single-token autoregressive loop, measured by TPOT (time per output token; equivalently the mean ITL, inter-token latency); each step reads the cached K/V, appends the new K/V, and samples the next token.'
findings.issue: The caption correctly states TTFT includes more than prefill, and the 'persistent KV cache' box is explicitly labelled as a conceptual grouping ('not runtime components: a real serving stack has per-layer, per-request KV state'). The defect is that the figure's box inventory does not match the book's own causal chain or the caption's own claim: the diagram contains 'PREFILL', 'PERSISTENT KV CACHE' and 'DECODE' plus 'prompt (given) tokens + positions', 'transformer', 'logits + sampling', 'first token', 'sampled token (prior step)', 'token + position (one per step)', 'next token' — with no box for retrieval, admission/queue, tokenization or transfer, all of which the book's TTFT convention (Preface p. 19; Ch. 2 p. 36) requires: 'TTFTe2e = retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill'. The figure's 'TTFT' attribution therefore cannot be verified against the convention the caption itself invokes, and a reader cannot see where the canonical ~120 ms retrieval sits in the pipeline.
findings.fix_instruction: Add the missing front-end boxes to Fig 2.1 (retrieval; admission/queue; tokenization/transfer) with a bracket marking them as outside the model's prefill but inside TTFT_e2e, so the figure matches the book's stated four-term TTFT convention.

findings.chapter: Ch. 2 What Actually Happens During Inference (and Ch. 4)
findings.evidence: p.46: 'case (iii) 2NL plus the causal-triangle attention term 2 · nlayers · L2 · d — stated here at first use, defined in full at Ch 8 §8.3.3'; p.49: '(a single request monopolizing the host; not the per-host aggregate rate of ~19,800 tok/s — see Ch 8 §8.3.4)'; Preface p.20: 'Do not repeat a chapter number after the chapter name — write Ch. 8 § 3 or § 8.3.3, not Ch. 8 § 8.3.3'; Ch.4 p.110: 'which Ch 8 Table 8-1 prints as ~2,472'
findings.issue: The body violates the book's own codified cross-reference convention twice in Ch. 2 by repeating the chapter number inside the section reference ('Ch 8 §8.3.3', 'Ch 8 §8.3.4'), and Ch. 4 repeats it before the table number ('Ch 8 Table 8-1' — the table number already carries the chapter prefix). The targets resolve correctly, so this is a form defect, but it is the exact form the Preface forbids and tells the reader to rely on.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite as '§ 8.3.3' / '§ 8.3.4' (or 'Ch. 8 § 3') on pp. 46 and 49, and 'Table 8-1' on p. 110; sweep Chs. 9–26 and Appendix A (not provided in this extract) for further 'Ch N §N.M' instances.
